title: Al-Halim, the Forbearing
hookLine: the Forbearing, who doesn't rush to punish

cards: Somebody cuts you off in traffic, and your thumb is already on the horn. A message lands in the group chat that's clearly about you, and your reply is half typed before you've finished reading. Anger is fast.
People often end up admiring the ones with a gap in them, a pause between the sting and the answer: you say something awful, and they wait, and they don't hand it back.
Scholars of early Arabic poetry say old Arabia had a word for that pause, and prized it in its chiefs. The Qur'an takes that word and makes it a name of God. Today: Al-Halim.

teach.b: Al-Halim comes from hilm. In old Arabia, hilm was the great virtue of a leader: calm, self-control, the power to hold back when you could strike.
Its opposite was jahl. Jahl is usually translated as ignorance, but in the old poems it often means hot-headedness, the man who flies off the handle and starts a feud over an insult.
So al-Halim is the One who sees every wrong, has all the power to answer it at once, and doesn't rush.
The Qur'an says it plainly: if God took people to task right away for everything they earned, he wouldn't leave a single creature walking on the earth.
Instead, he gives time: time to notice, time to turn around. Muslims hear forbearance in that delay, not indifference: al-Halim sees, and waits, because the waiting leaves the door open.
The name often sits beside forgiving: first he holds back, then he forgives. And hilm is a name a person can grow into. The Qur'an calls Abraham halim.

When a chief named al-Ashajj came to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ with his people, the Prophet told him, in a hadith in Sahih Muslim, that he had two qualities God loves: hilm, forbearance, and anah, taking your time.
Another man asked the Prophet for advice and was told, don't get angry; when he asked again, the same answer, again.
Not that anger never comes. It just doesn't get to drive.

how: Muslims name God as al-Halim, often alongside al-Ghafur, the Forgiving, and many take the Prophet's advice not to get angry as a daily discipline, pausing, sitting down or making wudu when anger rises.

o: the one who punishes every wrong fairly
the one who never notices wrongs at all
the one who sees every wrong and doesn't rush

games.q: what's inside the name — tap the pairs.
p: praised for hilm and taking time
the advice, given again and again

s: jahl in the old Arabic poems often means hot-headedness
not only ignorance: the man who flies off the handle. hilm is its opposite.
al-Halim means God doesn't notice wrongs
he sees every wrong and has the power to answer, and still gives time.
hilm is a name a person can grow into.

games.q: a man asks the Prophet for one piece of advice. he gets it, and asks again, hoping for more. what does he hear the second time?
o: the same thing: don't get angry.
games.why: don't get angry, again, and again. the advice was short because it was the whole point.

practice: Bring back a moment from this week when something stung, and feel how fast the answer wanted to come.
Now put a gap there, one slow breath in and one slow breath out, and only then picture what you'd say, noticing whether it's different; run it once more with another moment.
If you pray, you can ask God, al-Halim, for a little of his hilm.

wordCard.voice: Al-Halim. The Forbearing: the One who sees every wrong, holds all the power, and doesn't rush to punish. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the Forbearing. from hilm, the calm self-control old Arabia prized in its chiefs.

carryVoice: Your line: slow to anger. One breath between the sting and the answer. Two hundred fifty days now.

sources.ref: Qur'an 35:45; 16:61 (if God took people to task at once, no creature would be left; he gives respite)
